name: North Tarrant Express (NTE)
limits: I-35W in north Fort Worth east along I-820 and SH 121/183 to near DFW Airport, 13.3 miles

equity_owners.name: Cintra (Ferrovial N.V., Amsterdam; listed Madrid, Amsterdam, Nasdaq)

toll_setting: Contract cap of $0.75 per mile (2009 dollars), raised every January by CPI. After the first 180 days the operator must run dynamic pricing and may change rates every 5 minutes. The cap is soft: when volume passes 3,300 vehicles per hour (2 lanes) or 5,100 (3 lanes), or speed drops under 50 mph, the operator may raise the rate up to 25% per 5-minute step with no upper limit. HOV 2+ pay half at peak. Trucks pay 3 to 5 times the car rate.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Section 11.3, 'Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facilities': if TxDOT builds a new limited-access main lane inside the corridor footprint that was not already in the 2006 STIP, UTP or Mobility 2030 plan, it owes the operator the lost toll revenue. Verbatim: 'The Compensation Amount, if any, owing from TxDOT to Developer on account of the Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facility shall be equal to the loss of Toll Revenues, if any, attributable to the Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facility.' TxDOT keeps the right to build anything, and the operator waives any right to block a project; it can only claim money.

revenue_latest.source: Ferrovial Integrated Annual Report 2025, Business Performance p. 36

notable: Texas's first privately run managed-lane corridor. In 2025 it took in $323 million and paid $216 million in dividends to its Spanish and French owners, an 86% margin on earnings before interest, tax and depreciation. Average revenue per trip rose 13.4% in 2025 to $8.70 and another 18.9% in the first half of 2026 to $10.10, while traffic fell. Cumulative dividends since opening: about $1.17 billion. Cintra bought out the Dallas Police and Fire Pension's stake in 2017 for $65 million. TxDOT received $8.1 million in revenue sharing in 2025. Contract runs to 2061.
ownership_source: Ferrovial Consolidated Financial Statements 2025, Note 5.1.4 (p. 383) and Fact Book 2026, slide 32
toll_setting_source: NTE CDA (June 23, 2009), Exhibit 4 Toll Regulation, sections C.1 and F.5

buyout.summary: No fixed price schedule. TxDOT pays the smaller of appraised fair market value (floored at senior debt) or senior debt plus projected future equity distributions topped up to a 23% equity IRR, in cash, or the termination is void.
buyout.source: NTE CDA Exhibit 20, sections A.1, B.1-B.3; Section 19.1.1

name: NTE 35W (North Tarrant Express Segments 3)
limits: I-30 in downtown Fort Worth north to Eagle Parkway at Alliance, about 17 miles

equity_owners.name: Cintra (Ferrovial N.V., Amsterdam; listed Madrid, Amsterdam, Nasdaq)

toll_setting: Contract cap of $0.75 per mile (2009 dollars), raised every January by CPI. Dynamic pricing is mandatory after the first 180 days, with rate changes allowed every 5 minutes. The cap is soft: when volume passes 3,300 vehicles per hour (2 lanes) or 5,100 (3 lanes), or speed drops under 50 mph, the operator may multiply the rate by up to 1.25 per step with no upper limit. Trucks pay 3 to 5 times the car rate.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Section 11.3, 'Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facilities': if TxDOT builds a new limited-access main lane inside the I-35W corridor footprint that was not already in the 2011-2014 STIP, 2013 UTP or Mobility 2035 plan, it owes the operator the lost toll revenue. Verbatim: 'The Compensation Amount, if any, owing from TxDOT to Developer on account of the Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facility shall be equal to the loss of Toll Revenues, if any, attributable to the Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facility.' Frontage roads, safety work and planned projects are carved out. The operator 'irrevocably waives' any right to block a project.

revenue_latest.source: Ferrovial Integrated Annual Report 2025, Business Performance p. 36

notable: The biggest earner of the three DFW concessions: $368 million in 2025, up 14.7% with traffic up only 2.9%, and $215 million paid out in dividends (another $143 million in the first half of 2026 alone). Average revenue per trip rose 11.6% in 2025 and 17.3% in the first half of 2026. Segment 3C to Alliance ($910 million, opened 2023) was added to the existing contract without a new bid. In June 2025 the company issued $457 million in bonds to pay off its federal TIFIA loan. TxDOT received $26.4 million in revenue sharing in 2025. The Dallas Police and Fire Pension sold its stake in 2016; the lanes are now 100% owned by Spanish, Dutch and French investors. Contract runs to 2061.
ownership_source: Ferrovial Consolidated Financial Statements 2025, Note 5.1.4 (p. 383) and Fact Book 2026, slide 32
toll_setting_source: NTE 35W Amended and Restated Facility Agreement (2019), Exhibit 4 Toll Regulation, sections C.1 and F.5

buyout.summary: TxDOT pays the smallest of a fixed schedule, appraised fair market value, or senior debt plus future distributions topped up to a 23% equity IRR, in cash within a year. The fixed schedule, measured from the 2019 Segment 3C amendment, is currently in its $7.4 billion interval and peaks at $15.6 billion in the 2040s.
buyout.verbatim: the Termination Compensation shall equal the smallest of the amounts determined as set forth in Sections B.2, B.3 and B.4 below.
buyout.source: NTE 35W A&R Facility Agreement, Exhibit 20 and Attachment 1 (Termination for Convenience Interval Pricing Amounts)
buyout.schedule_note: Intervals run from the 2019 Segment 3C amendment effective date.

name: LBJ Express (I-635 and I-35E)
limits: I-635 from Luna Road to Greenville Avenue plus I-35E from Loop 12 to I-635, about 17 miles

equity_owners.name: Cintra (Ferrovial N.V., Amsterdam; listed Madrid, Amsterdam, Nasdaq)

toll_setting: Contract cap of $0.75 per mile (2009 dollars), raised every January by CPI. Dynamic pricing mandatory after the first 180 days, changes allowed every 5 minutes. Soft cap: above 3,300 vehicles per hour (2 lanes) or 5,100 (3 lanes), or under 50 mph, the operator may raise rates up to 25% per step with no upper limit. NTTA collects the tolls.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Section 11.3, 'Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facilities', identical in structure to NTE: TxDOT owes the operator lost toll revenue if it builds a new unplanned limited-access main lane inside the corridor footprint. Verbatim: 'The Compensation Amount ... shall be equal to the loss of Toll Revenues, if any, attributable to the Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facility less the increase in Toll Revenues, if any, attributable to (a) the Unplanned Revenue Impacting Facilities.' The operator can only claim money, never block a project.

revenue_latest.source: Ferrovial Integrated Annual Report 2025, Business Performance p. 36

notable: The $2.6 billion elevated toll lanes through north Dallas carry $2.04 billion in debt and earned $244 million in 2025 with flat traffic but 8.7% more per trip; the first half of 2026 added another 11.7% per trip. $123 million went to owners in 2025, about $952 million since opening. The Dallas Police and Fire Pension sold its stake in 2017 for $42 million. Contract runs to 2061.
ownership_source: Ferrovial Consolidated Financial Statements 2025, Note 5.1.4 (p. 383) and Fact Book 2026, slide 32
toll_setting_source: LBJ (IH 635 Managed Lanes) CDA (Sept 4, 2009), Exhibit 4 Toll Regulation, sections C.1 and F.5

buyout.summary: No fixed price schedule. TxDOT pays the smaller of appraised fair market value (floored at senior debt) or senior debt plus future equity distributions topped up to a 23% equity IRR.
buyout.source: LBJ CDA Exhibit 23, sections A.1, B.1; Section 19.1

name: SH 130 Segments 5 and 6
limits: SH 45 SE south of Austin to I-10 at Seguin, 41 miles, the 85 mph road

equity_owners.name: Strategic Value Partners (hedge fund) and affiliates
U.S. Department of Transportation (via TIFIA debt-to-equity in the 2017 bankruptcy plan)

toll_setting: Maximum toll rate is indexed to nominal Texas gross state product per capita, and the index can only go up ('the greater of NGSP(t)/PC(t) or NGSPPC(t-1)'). 2006 base rates per mile: cars 12.5 cents, car with trailer 25 cents, large trucks 37.5 to 62.5 cents. The operator may change rates at any time below the cap.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: No compensation clause for competing roads found in the executed text (Exhibit 17 not reviewed). Instead the operator shares revenue with TxDOT in three bands, set when Texas chose the 85 mph speed limit: 11.05% of annual tolls in Band 1, 22.1% in Band 2, 50% above Band 3. Band thresholds are in 2006 dollars adjusted by CPI and grow every year (Band 1 ceiling about $125 million in year 14, $170 million in year 20), so the 50% tier is unlikely to be reached. Upfront payment: $25 million. TxDOT could have taken a $100 million lump sum for 85 mph instead of the higher sharing tiers.
notable: Texas's first private toll road, built by Cintra and Zachry, went bankrupt in 2016 when traffic missed forecasts. The 2017 plan erased $1.4 billion of debt and handed the road to hedge fund SVP, with the federal government ending up owning about a third. Texas sold the nation's highest speed limit for a $100 million payment. Revenue has since boomed. In 2025 a bill to extend the concession 20 years to 2082 passed the Texas House 76-45 and died in the Senate.

buyout.summary: No fixed price schedule in this 2007 deal. TxDOT may terminate at will but must first pay compensation based on a final appraisal (Exhibit 22).
buyout.verbatim: TxDOT may terminate this Agreement and the Lease in whole, but not in part, if TxDOT, in its sole discretion, elects to do so

revenue_note: Annual revenue is not public: the post-bankruptcy debt is privately placed, so there are no bond disclosures. Last public figures: 11.42 million transactions in 2022 (+17%), a record again in 2023. A Public Information Act request to TxDOT for the annual Exhibit 7 revenue-share certification would give the exact number.

name: SH 288 Toll Lanes (bought back by TxDOT, 2024)
limits: I-69 near downtown Houston south to the Brazoria County line, 10.3 miles of median toll lanes
operator: Blueridge Transportation Group, LLC (2016 to Oct 2024); TxDOT since October 8, 2024
toll_setting: Under the concession the operator set dynamic tolls. TxDOT kept variable pricing after the buyback with a 45 mph target and says rates will fall well below what the contract allowed. First TxDOT year (FY2025) revenue: $107.35 million.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Exhibit 20 fixed the buyout price by interval. TxDOT paid the 'years 2-4' amount of $1,731,730,721 on October 8, 2024. Had it waited past November 2024 the price would have been $1,935,523,307, and it would have kept rising to a peak of $4.9 billion in years 28-30. The 2013 law (SB 1730) that required these schedules does not cover the 2009 NTE and LBJ contracts.
notable: The only Texas concession ever bought back. On October 8, 2024 TxDOT paid $1,731,730,721 to end a 52-year deal eight years in, funded by toll revenue bonds maturing in 2064. Abertis got $688 million; ACS got $524 million. Governor Abbott called it 'a $4 billion asset for $1.7 billion.' Anti-toll legislators attacked TxDOT for keeping tolls on a road the state now owns.

buyout.summary: Paid: $1,731,730,721 on October 8, 2024, the 'years 2-4' interval price. Confirmed by Texas Transportation Commission Minute Order, July 30, 2024, item 10.
buyout.verbatim: the department intends to make, or cause to be made, a payment to the developer in the amount of $1,731,730,721 (termination payment)
buyout.source: SH 288 CDA (March 4, 2016) Exhibit 20; TTC Minute Order 2024-07-30 item 10
buyout.schedule_note: Intervals run from the November 2020 opening.

name: Indiana Toll Road (ITR)
limits: 157 mi across northern Indiana from the Illinois line (Chicago Skyway) to the Ohio line (Ohio Turnpike)

equity_owners.name: IFM Investors (IFM Global Infrastructure Fund) - lead/majority

toll_setting: Concession agreement sets rate schedule; annual escalation at the greater of 2%, CPI or nominal GDP per capita growth (since 2010); ITRCC applies increases each July 1. Flat distance-based tolls, not dynamic.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation event if the state builds a competing limited-access highway of 20+ miles within 10 miles of the ITR (limited exceptions); state also must compensate for toll freezes it imposed (e.g., 2006-2016 passenger ETC freeze funded by state).
buyout: Standard termination-for-convenience with compensation at fair market value/debt plus equity return; not exercised. Original concessionaire (Cintra/Macquarie) went bankrupt in 2014 and the lease was resold for $5.725B in 2015 for the remaining 66 years.
notable: First state lease of an existing US toll road: a 75-year lease for $3.8B in 2006 to Spain's Cintra and Australia's Macquarie, which filed Chapter 11 in 2014 after traffic missed forecasts. Australian pension manager IFM bought the remaining 66 years for $5.725B in 2015 and later brought in CDPQ, CalPERS and Allstate. Tolls now rise every July under a formula tied to CPI/GDP; passenger-car full-length toll exceeds $15 (2025).
match_hint: Route I-90 (and I-80/I-90 overlap west of Elkhart), state FIPS 18; counties Lake, Porter, LaPorte, St. Joseph, Elkhart, LaGrange, Steuben. Full tolled facility, entire mainline.

name: Chicago Skyway
limits: 7.8 mi elevated toll road from I-94 Dan Ryan Expressway to the Indiana state line / Indiana Toll Road
toll_setting: Concession schedule set fixed caps through 2017; thereafter annual increases capped at the greatest of 2%, CPI, or nominal GDP per capita growth. Car toll rose again on Jan 1 2025 and Jan 1 2026 (above $7). Flat, not dynamic.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: City may not build competing facilities that materially divert traffic without compensation; standard adverse-action compensation.
buyout: City termination rights with compensation of fair market value; never exercised.

revenue_latest.source: Atlas Arteria FY2025 results (ASX, 26 Feb 2026): Chicago Skyway toll revenue US$137.9m, EBITDA US$114.8m, net debt US$1,555m

notable: First long-term lease of an existing US toll road (99 years, $1.83B, 2005) to Cintra/Macquarie, who flipped it to three Canadian pension funds for $2.8B in 2016; Australia's Atlas Arteria then bought 66.67% for about US$2.0B in 2022. 2025 toll revenue was US$138m on 12.7m trips, an 83% EBITDA margin, with debt of US$1.56B. The lease runs to 2104.
match_hint: Route I-90, state FIPS 17, Cook County, City of Chicago; full tolled facility between the Dan Ryan (I-94) interchange and the Indiana line.

name: Dulles Greenway
limits: 14 mi from the Dulles Toll Road terminus at Dulles Airport (Route 28) west to US 15 at Leesburg, Loudoun County
operator: Toll Road Investors Partnership II, L.P. (TRIP II)
toll_setting: Regulated by the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) under the 1988 Highway Corporation Act. 2013-2020 formula allowed annual increases at the greater of CPI+1%, real GDP, or 2.8%; since 2020 increases require SCC approval. SCC rejected the 2021/2024 rate cases; Virginia Supreme Court upheld the denial (2025); TRIP II's federal suit was dismissed (June 2026); new rate case filed Dec 2025 under revised 2025 state law allowing two-year applications. Distance-based with peak/off-peak pricing; one-way car toll roughly $5-6 at peak (2024-25).
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: No formal non-compete; Loudoun County has long sought a public buyout or toll relief. Legislature extended term 20 years (to 2056) in 2001 after near-default.
buyout: Facility reverts to the Commonwealth in 2056 at no cost. Periodic Loudoun/Virginia proposals to buy out TRIP II have not advanced; Atlas Arteria disclosed US$913m net debt against US$83.5m revenue in 2025.

revenue_latest.source: Atlas Arteria FY2025 results (ASX, 26 Feb 2026): Dulles Greenway toll revenue US$83.5m, traffic 15.0m, EBITDA US$65.3m, net debt US$913.2m

notable: The first private toll road built in the US since the 1800s (1995), now wholly owned by Australia's Atlas Arteria. It has some of the highest per-mile tolls in the country and has lost repeated rate-increase fights with Virginia regulators and courts (2023-2026). Carries roughly US$913m of debt on US$83.5m of 2025 revenue; the state gets it back free in 2056.
match_hint: Route VA-267 west of Route 28, state FIPS 51, Loudoun County (FIPS 107). Full tolled facility; note VA-267 east of Route 28 is the publicly owned Dulles Toll Road (MWAA), exclude it.

name: Pocahontas Parkway (Route 895) and Richmond Airport Connector
limits: 8.8 mi from I-95/Chippenham Parkway (Chesterfield County) across the James River to I-295 near Richmond International Airport (Henrico County), plus 1.6 mi airport connector
toll_setting: Fixed point-to-point tolls by class per the 2006 Amended and Restated Comprehensive Agreement, with scheduled increases and CPI-linked escalation thereafter (exact formula not re-verified); not dynamic. Car toll about $4+ (2024).
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation for VDOT-built competing facilities within a defined zone; standard adverse-action clause.
buyout: VDOT may terminate for convenience with compensation. Transurban wrote the asset down to zero and surrendered it to lenders (DBi Services) in 2014; Globalvia bought it in 2016 for roughly $611m.
notable: Built in 1998-2002 by a nonprofit 63-20 corporation whose bonds failed on weak traffic; Australia's Transurban bought a 99-year concession in 2006 for $611m, then wrote it off and handed it to lenders in 2014. Spanish operator Globalvia (owned by Canadian, Dutch and UK pension funds) took it in 2016. Concession runs to 2105.
match_hint: Route VA-895, state FIPS 51, Chesterfield (041) and Henrico (087) counties; full tolled facility.

name: Elizabeth River Tunnels (Midtown Tunnel, Downtown Tunnel, MLK Extension)
limits: Midtown Tunnel (US 58) and Downtown Tunnel (I-264) between Norfolk and Portsmouth, plus the 0.8-mi MLK Freeway (VA-164) extension to I-264 in Portsmouth
toll_setting: Concession sets maximum tolls with annual escalation of the greater of CPI or 3.5% (peak/off-peak differential, trucks by axle). Virginia has twice bought down tolls with public money (2016 toll relief program; HOV2+ free pilot 2024). Not dynamic.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation event if VDOT adds competing untolled river crossings or capacity (e.g., a third Hampton Roads crossing) that diverts traffic; tolling of pre-existing tunnels was contested in court (Elizabeth River Crossings v. Meeks, 2013, upheld).
buyout: VDOT termination for convenience at agreed compensation; Skanska (50%) sold to Abertis/Manulife for $625m in 2020 (total deal $2.3B incl. debt).
notable: Virginia let a private consortium toll two existing, previously free tunnels to pay for a new parallel Midtown tube; the concession runs 58 years to 2070 with tolls escalating at least 3.5% a year. Spain's Abertis (68%) and Canada's Manulife bought the deal for about US$2.3B in 2020, a windfall for Skanska and Macquarie. Tolls have been politically toxic in Portsmouth, prompting repeated state-funded relief.
match_hint: US-58 (Midtown Tunnel) and I-264 (Downtown Tunnel) river crossings, state FIPS 51, independent cities Norfolk (710) and Portsmouth (740); tolled only at the tunnels (not full-corridor), plus VA-164 MLK Extension segment.

name: 495 Express Lanes (Capital Beltway HOT lanes) incl. 495 NEXT northern extension
limits: Springfield Interchange (I-95/I-395) north to the Dulles Toll Road (14 mi), extended 2.5 mi north to the George Washington Parkway/American Legion Bridge (495 NEXT, opened 2025)
toll_setting: Fully dynamic, uncapped congestion pricing set by the concessionaire (HOV3+ free with E-ZPass Flex); revenue sharing with VDOT kicks in above return thresholds. Peak tolls above $30 for the 14-mile trip have been recorded.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: VDOT must compensate if it adds free capacity within the corridor or if HOV3+ free use exceeds 24% of traffic in a period (HOV compensation clause).
buyout: Termination for convenience at fair market value including equity return; 2014 debt restructuring injected $280m equity after weak early revenue.
notable: First dynamically priced HOT lanes in Virginia and the first US use of private activity bonds for managed lanes. Owned 50% by Australia's Transurban and 50% by Australian and Canadian pension funds, with the concession lasting until 2087. The contract makes Virginia pay Transurban if too many carpoolers ride free.
match_hint: I-495 managed lanes within the free Beltway, state FIPS 51, Fairfax County (059), from the Springfield Interchange to the American Legion Bridge; managed lanes only (general purpose lanes are untolled).

name: 95 Express Lanes / 395 Express Lanes / Fredericksburg Extension
limits: Reversible express lanes about 50 mi from Route 17 near Fredericksburg (Stafford/Spotsylvania line) north along I-95 and I-395 to the Potomac River at the DC line
toll_setting: Fully dynamic congestion pricing set by the concessionaire, no cap; HOV3+ free. Concessionaire pays VDOT $15m/yr (escalating) for I-395 transit and paid a $277m 'Permit Fee Buyout' in 2019 to eliminate future revenue sharing.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation if VDOT adds competing free capacity or if HOV share exceeds thresholds (similar to 495). Original 2012 plan dropped Arlington segment after Arlington County lawsuit.
buyout: Termination for convenience with compensation; concession extended/amended three times (395 in 2017, Fredericksburg 2019, Opitz Blvd 2022) rather than reprocured.
notable: Roughly 50 miles of reversible dynamically priced lanes from Fredericksburg to the Pentagon, all controlled by one Australian-led company under a concession running to 2087. In 2019 Transurban paid Virginia $277m to buy out the state's future share of toll revenue in exchange for the Fredericksburg extension. Transurban reported US revenue up 14% in FY2026.
match_hint: I-95 and I-395 managed (reversible) lanes within free interstates, state FIPS 51; counties Stafford (179), Prince William (153), Fairfax (059), cities Alexandria (510), Arlington (013). Managed lanes only.

name: 66 Express Outside the Beltway (Transform 66)
limits: 22.5 mi of I-66 from I-495 Capital Beltway west to US 29 in Gainesville, Prince William County; two express lanes each direction

equity_owners.name: Meridiam Infrastructure North America Fund II
John Laing (remaining stake, may have exited)

toll_setting: Fully dynamic, uncapped congestion pricing set by the concessionaire; HOV3+ free. Concessionaire also owes NPV $800m for corridor transit and $350m for other corridor projects over the term.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation events for competing VDOT capacity; HOV compensation threshold similar to 495/95 (no HOV2 free). Inside-the-Beltway segment is tolled by VDOT itself (public).
buyout: VDOT termination for convenience with compensation. Cintra raised its stake from 50% to 55.7% in 2021 for US$181.9m.
notable: The only big US toll concession where the private side paid the state (about $579m upfront, FHWA cites ~$500m) rather than the reverse, financed with $1.5B of equity and a $1.23B TIFIA loan. Majority owned by Spain's Ferrovial/Cintra with French and Dutch pension capital; term 50 years to 2066. Ferrovial reported I-66 traffic +7.4% and revenue per trip +13.3% in 2025.
match_hint: I-66 managed lanes within the free interstate, state FIPS 51, Fairfax (059) and Prince William (153) counties, from I-495 to US 29 Gainesville; managed lanes only. Exclude I-66 inside the Beltway (public VDOT tolling).

name: I-77 Express Lanes (Charlotte)
limits: 26 mi from I-277 uptown Charlotte north to Exit 36 (NC 150) in Mooresville, Mecklenburg and Iredell counties

equity_owners.name: abrdn (Aberdeen Global Infrastructure Partners II) - may have sold

toll_setting: Dynamic pricing set by concessionaire, no cap; HOV3+ free. Includes a Developer Ratio Adjustment Mechanism (state backstop up to $75m if revenues fall short) and revenue sharing above return thresholds.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: NCDOT must compensate for added free general-purpose capacity in the corridor; the Lake Norman area's single-lane section has been a flashpoint. 2026 MOU under which Cintra would study adding a second toll lane north of Cornelius.
buyout: 2018-2019 state studies put a buyout at roughly $300m+ plus lost-revenue claims; legislature did not fund it. NCDOT also owes $64m repayment of design costs if it ends the deal.
notable: Charlotte's most-hated highway project: a 50-year concession to Spain's Cintra with uncapped dynamic tolls that helped flip a 2016 state legislative seat and spurred a failed buyout push. Cintra raised its stake to 65.1% in 2020, and by mid-2026 had collected nearly half a billion dollars in tolls, with 43 years left. In 2026 NCDOT began talks on letting Cintra add a second toll lane rather than a free lane.
match_hint: I-77 (and I-277 ramp connections) managed lanes within a free interstate, state FIPS 37, Mecklenburg (119) and Iredell (097) counties; managed lanes only.

name: Northwest Parkway
limits: 8.9 mi from E-470 at I-25 (Broomfield/Adams line) west to 96th Street near US 36 in Broomfield
toll_setting: Concessionaire sets tolls within caps that escalate annually on a CPI-linked formula in the 2007 Concession and Lease Agreement (exact formula not re-verified); flat per-plaza tolls, all-electronic since 2017. Revenue sharing with the Authority above profit thresholds.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Yes: the Authority agreed to compensate for competing untolled improvements in a defined area, which delayed widening of nearby US 36 and local roads (the Broomfield/Jefferson Parkway dispute).
buyout: Authority termination with compensation; concession sold Brisa (Portugal) -> HICL/DIF/Northleaf (2017, ~$1.1B) -> VINCI Highways (2024).
notable: A 99-year lease (to 2106) of a failing public toll road in Denver's northern suburbs, first to Portugal's Brisa for $603m in 2007 and resold twice, most recently to France's VINCI in 2024. Its non-compete clause has constrained free road upgrades in Broomfield for years. 7.2m transactions in 2023.
match_hint: Northwest Parkway, state FIPS 08, Broomfield (014) and Adams (001) counties; full tolled facility. Note E-470 and C-470 are public (do not match).

name: US 36 Express Lanes and I-25 Express Lanes (Denver-Boulder)
limits: US 36 HOT lanes from I-25 (Denver) to Table Mesa Dr./Foothills Pkwy in Boulder (16 mi) plus the existing I-25 Express Lanes between US 36 and downtown Denver (20th St) and north to 120th Ave
toll_setting: Dynamic/time-of-day pricing within caps set by the concession agreement, approved by CDOT's HPTE/CTIO; HOV3+ free. Concessionaire keeps toll revenue from US 36 and I-25 express lanes with revenue sharing above thresholds.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation events for competing capacity; 2014 contract controversy over a non-compete/'alternative route' clause and a 50-year term signed with little public review led to Colorado P3 transparency legislation (2014).
buyout: HPTE termination for convenience with compensation; not exercised.
notable: Colorado's only revenue-risk highway concession: a 50-year deal signed in 2014 that hands Plenary (now owned by Quebec's CDPQ) toll revenue from US 36 and the pre-existing public I-25 HOV/toll lanes into downtown Denver. The secretive signing triggered a public backlash and a 2014 state P3 transparency law.
match_hint: US-36 managed lanes within a free highway, state FIPS 08, Adams (001), Broomfield (014), Jefferson (059), Boulder (013) counties; plus I-25 managed lanes Denver (031) and Adams counties between 20th St and 120th Ave. Managed lanes only.

name: PR-22 (Jose de Diego Expressway) and PR-5 (Rio Hondo Expressway)
limits: PR-22 52 mi from San Juan west to Hatillo/Arecibo; PR-5 2.5 mi in Bayamon; includes dynamic toll lanes San Juan-Toa Baja
operator: Autopistas Metropolitanas de Puerto Rico LLC (Metropistas)
toll_setting: Concession agreement allows annual toll increases indexed to CPI (approx. CPI+1.5% in early years) on PR-22/PR-5; dynamic tolling on the reversible express lanes. Rates set by concessionaire within contract caps, overseen by the P3 Authority.
non_compete_or_compensation_clause: Compensation for competing government facilities and for government-imposed toll changes; 2016 extension raised concessionaire revenue share from 50% to 75%.
buyout: P3 Authority termination with compensation; 40-year term extended 10 years in 2016 for an extra $115m payment.
notable: Puerto Rico leased its busiest highway for 40 years in 2011 for $1.08B to Spain's Abertis and Goldman Sachs (Goldman's 49% later sold to US union fund Ullico in 2020), then added 10 more years in 2016 for $115m while boosting the private revenue share to 75%. Concession now runs to 2061.
match_hint: PR-22 and PR-5, state FIPS 72 (Puerto Rico), municipios San Juan, Guaynabo, Bayamon, Toa Baja, Dorado, Vega Alta, Vega Baja, Manati, Barceloneta, Arecibo, Hatillo. Full tolled facility (PR-22 counts as unsigned Interstate PRI-2).

name: Puerto Rico Toll Roads Monetization (PR-52, PR-20, PR-53, PR-66)
limits: 144 mi: PR-52 San Juan-Ponce (Autopista Luis A. Ferre), PR-20 Guaynabo, PR-53 Fajardo-Salinas segments, PR-66 Carolina-Rio Grande
operator: Puerto Rico Toll Roads LLC (Abertis subsidiary, operated under the Metropistas brand)
